Problems & solutions

How do I get back into exercise after months or years away?

Choose a starting point based on where you are today.

By Nutrition.Fitness · 15 September 2026 · 4 min read

The short answer

Return at a level you can manage now, rather than trying to repeat what you did years ago. Choose an activity you can access easily, begin with modest sessions and build gradually according to how you respond. Make the first aim a repeatable routine. If you have been inactive for a long time or have health concerns, speak to a GP before starting.

Start with what your body and diary can manage now. Your old running pace, gym weights or five-day schedule are background information, not instructions for the first week back.

It is tempting to make the return dramatic. New kit, a demanding programme and a promise to train every morning can feel like a fresh start. A quieter start often makes the practical questions easier to answer: can you get there, can you do the activity comfortably, and can you return?

Check what has changed

Consider why you stopped and what is different today. Time, caring responsibilities, injury, illness, confidence, money and enjoyment can all affect the choice. If you stopped because the gym journey was impossible, buying the same membership may not solve it.

The NHS advises speaking to a GP first if you have not exercised for some time or have medical conditions or concerns. Returning after surgery, significant illness or an injury may require specific professional guidance rather than a generic beginner plan.

This check is about selecting an appropriate start. You do not have to prove that you are already fit before seeking help to become active.

Choose an easy place to begin

You might choose a short walk, a beginner class, swimming, accessible home movement or a gym induction. The best opening choice is one you can realistically access and feel willing to repeat. Enjoyment and convenience deserve a place in the decision.

If the main difficulty is...Consider starting with...
Travel and childcareAn activity from home, with a protected time agreed in the household
Confidence using equipmentA supported induction or individual instruction
Not knowing what to doA clear beginner sequence, with instructions and easier options
Being aloneA friend, local group or suitable beginner class
An ongoing injury or health issueAppropriate clinical or rehabilitation guidance

Make the first fortnight a practical trial

Choose a small number of opportunities you can protect in the diary. Keep the opening sessions modest enough that you can learn how they fit. If ten minutes is your appropriate starting point, there is no reason to add another twenty merely because a video continues.

After each session, record two things: how the activity felt and what made attendance easy or awkward. “Walked from home after lunch; fine, but needed a coat” tells you what to do next. You do not need a complicated dashboard.

In the second week, repeat the parts that worked. If it feels appropriate, make one small adjustment, such as a little more duration or practice. You can also repeat the same level. The purpose of a trial is to learn, not to force improvement on a deadline.

Do not use soreness as the success measure

You are looking for a routine that fits and activities you can perform appropriately. Finishing exhausted does not prove that you selected the right starting point. Nor does an easy first session mean it was pointless.

Stop if an exercise causes pain or you feel unwell. Persistent pain or difficulty returning after illness should be assessed rather than repeatedly worked around through internet advice. Tell an instructor about relevant limitations so they can stay within their scope and refer appropriately.

If you were previously experienced, consider asking for a refresher. Familiarity can make it easy to select a resistance or pace based on memory. There is no embarrassment in checking technique after a long break.

You may not need a paid programme yet

If you want to start running and it is appropriate for you, NHS Couch to 5K is a free beginner option. It alternates running and walking, includes rest days and can take longer than nine weeks. You do not have to finish to a date or run five kilometres at a particular speed.

If you want strength instruction, an initial session with a qualified professional might solve more than buying a large collection of workouts. If you mostly need a walking companion, ask a friend. Choose the form of support that addresses the obstacle.

What should a paid plan show you?

Look for the starting level, equipment, session duration, options for adapting exercises and the route to getting help. Ask how you return after missing a week. Check whether advice comes from a qualified person, a prerecorded resource or AI; these are different types of support.

You can explore the Nutrition.Fitness programme pages, while checking current availability and scope before committing. A suitable plan should reduce uncertainty, not ask you to ignore it. What stopped you last time, and what would make that obstacle smaller now?

Sources and checks

Information checked on 15 September 2026.

  • NHS: Physical activity guidelines for adults aged 19 to 64
  • NHS: Get running with Couch to 5K
